1:
The naming of Josiah three centuries before his birth is the chapter's great question, and the two who face it come down on opposite sides. Clarke treats it as among the most remarkable prophecies in the Old Testament, circumstantially foretelling a fact which took place three hundred and forty years after the prediction, and he argues its authenticity from the adversarial interest of the parties: a fact attested by two nations, the Jews guarding most sacredly a prophecy delivered in their behalf, and the Israelites, against whom it was levelled, having every interest in exposing its falsehood had that been possible. Ellicott grants the particularity, calling this one of the rather unfrequent prophecies not content to foreshadow the future in general outline but descending to striking particularity of detail; but he reports the suggestion that the words Josiah by name are a marginal gloss which has crept into the text, or an insertion by the chronicler writing after the event, and says of the second that it is in itself not unlikely. He then defends the detail anyway, on two grounds: that the naming of a person in prediction is exemplified in the well-known reference to Cyrus, and that the name here is significant, since Josiah means one healed or helped by Jehovah, and so is not a mere artificial detail.

Who the man of God was is a second question where the sources agree in conclusion and differ in reasons. Ellicott reports that Josephus calls him Jadon, that is Iddo, but shows the identification impossible from the chronology, since Iddo was the chronicler of Abijah's reign and must have lived until near the close of Jeroboam's; he suspects the tradition came from a mistaken reading of the visions of Iddo against Jeroboam. Gill reaches the same verdict from the narrative, since this man was quickly slain whereas Iddo lived on after Rehoboam and wrote his acts first and last, and he rules out Shemaiah for the same reason, though an early writer names him. Ellicott adds that the English weakens the original, which has the prophet speak not by but in the word of the Lord, so that he came clothed in the inspiration of the word put into his mouth.

Henry reads the sending as a mercy rather than a threat. The army of Judah that aimed to ruin Jeroboam had been countermanded, and a prophet was sent instead to reclaim him from his evil way, and sent in time, while he was only dedicating his altar and before his heart was hardened by the deceitfulness of his sin, for God delights not in the death of sinners. He admires the courage of it, since those who go on God's errand must not fear the face of man, knowing who will bear them out, and notices that the message was cried with a loud voice and addressed neither to Jeroboam nor to the people but to the altar, whose stones would sooner hear and yield than men mad upon their idols and deaf to divine calls; yet in threatening the altar God threatened its founder and worshippers, who might conclude that if his wrath fastens on the lifeless guiltless altar they cannot escape. Henry turns the prediction into an irony, that the priests of the high places should themselves be made sacrifices to the justice of God, the first and only sacrifices on that altar that would please him. Clarke supplies the physical detail, that the arm became suddenly rigid, the nerves no longer communicating their influence and the muscles ceasing to obey the will, and that the altar split of its own accord so the ashes were poured out; and he notes the king's own words, entreat the face of the Lord thy God, since Jeroboam knew he was not his own God, being then in the act of acknowledging others.
11:
What the old prophet was draws three verdicts. Henry will not soften it: he cannot but call him a false prophet and a bad man, since it is easier to believe a confirmation was extorted from a bad character than that a true prophet should tell so deliberate a lie and father it upon God. He supposes the man trained among the sons of the prophets, retaining the name while the spirit of prophecy had departed, and judges the design bad, to draw the man of God into a snare, false prophets having ever been the worst enemies of the true, sometimes aiming to destroy and sometimes to debauch them. Ellicott denies both halves: the narrative implies, and much of its instructiveness depends on it, that the old prophet was neither a pretender to inspiration nor an apostate, but one who like Balaam united true prophetic gifts with a low worldliness of temper capable of base subterfuge, such discordant elements being characteristic of man's self-contradictory nature; he had thrown in his lot with Jeroboam's policy and yet desired to remain a prophet of the Lord and support the king's action by prophetic influence. Clarke takes a third position, that he was once a prophet of the Lord fallen from his steadfastness yet not so deeply as to lose the knowledge of the true God, noting he was not himself at the king's sacrifice though his sons were; and on the motive he is mildest, saying he can hardly think there was any evil design, that curiosity about the prediction explains it, and that this good man could not have been an object of malevolence.

Why the man believed so gross a lie divides them again. Ellicott holds the belief culpable: the falsehood ought to have been obvious to one who had a plain command and knew that God is not a man that he should lie, and was believed because it chimed in with a secret reluctance to obey and so give up all reward and hospitality, so that the belief was self-deceit and as such blameable; he finds it inexplicable that the condemnation should seem strange to anyone who understands the self-deceiving colour our wish gives to our thought. Clarke floats an exculpation, that the man permitted himself to be imposed on and might have reasoned that, having accomplished all he was sent for and begun to return by another way, the God who gave the charge had authority to dispense with the rest of it, as with Abraham and Isaac. Ellicott had anticipated such leniency, noting that the oak where the man was found suggests a needless loitering.

The sharpest collision is over who pronounced sentence. Ellicott makes it the most terrible feature of the history that the divine sentence is spoken, unwillingly as in the case of Balaam, through the very lips which by falsehood had lured the prophet of Judah from the right path, and at the very table of treacherous hospitality; and he complains that Josephus, with his perverse tendency to explain away all that seems startling, misses the point by assigning the revelation to the prophet of Judah himself. Clarke makes that very move, reporting Kennicott's observation that a great clamour has been raised against this part of the history because God denounces sentence on the true prophet by the mouth of the false, and that the original words will bear either he who brought him back or whom he had brought back. Clarke adopts the escape, taking the speaker for the voice of God from heaven addressing the man of God, the old prophet having nothing to do in the business. Ellicott, far from avoiding the difficulty, generalises it into a law: the voice of worldly wisdom first beguiles the servants of God to disobedience by false glosses on their duty, then proclaims unsparingly their sin and its just punishment.
23:
Why the death was so severe for so small an offence is Henry's question, and he answers in two parts. First, the offence was great and the lie no excuse: he could not be as certain of a countermand sent through another as of the command given to himself, and had no ground to think it recalled while its reason remained, that he should testify his detestation of the place's wickedness; he had reason besides to suspect a prophet who did not bear his own testimony against the idolatry of his city, and should have begged direction from God rather than complying at once. Henry presses the excuses. Did he think the old prophet's house safer to eat in than any other at Bethel, when God had forbidden him to eat in any? That was to refine upon the command and make himself wiser than God. Did he plead hunger? Had he never read that man lives not by bread alone? Second, the death was for the glory of God, since two things appeared by it: that nothing provokes him more than disobedience to an express command though in a small matter, which makes his proceedings against our first parents the easier to account for; and that no man is protected in disobedience by the sanctity of his profession, the dignity of his office, or any good services done. Clarke reaches the same severity but keeps a mercy Henry does not mention, that the man committed the sin unto death, meaning such a sin as God punishes with the death of the body while extending mercy to the soul.

On the scene at the roadside Clarke and Ellicott work in different registers. Clarke insists on the miracle: all here was preternatural, since the lion though it killed the man does not devour him, the ass stands quietly by unafraid, and the lion does not tear the ass, both standing as guardians of the fallen prophet, so the hand of God is evident in all. Ellicott instead supplies natural history, that lions are mentioned in the Old Testament not unfrequently and especially in southern Palestine, and that now the forests have disappeared the lions have disappeared with them. On the old prophet's reaction Ellicott is acute: he did not know how his prediction was to be fulfilled but recognised its supernatural fulfilment at once, and there is a characteristic reticence about his own share in the business, both the deceit and the prediction, perhaps indicating the strange mixture of remorse and unscrupulous policy that comes out later. Clarke takes the request to be buried beside him as arguing a strong conviction that the dead man was holy, the old prophet being willing to have place with him in the general resurrection.

The cities of Samaria produce the chapter's historical difficulty, and Clarke sets it out squarely. It is most certain Samaria was not built at this time, since Omri founded it on a hill bought for two talents of silver from a man named Shemer, fifty years after Jeroboam's death. How then could the old prophet speak of Samaria? Clarke offers three answers without finally choosing: that he spoke by the spirit of prophecy, calling things that are not as though they were, as the man of God had named Josiah three centuries before his birth; that the historian added the words because Samaria existed in his own time; or, on Houbigant's solution, which many good critics think sound, that God gave the revelation and the prophet spoke by anticipation, the language of prophecy. On the sequel Ellicott draws an inference nobody else notices: the emphatic tone of whosoever would, he consecrated him, possibly indicates that in spite of all Jeroboam could do there was difficulty in finding candidates for the unauthorised priesthood. He takes the closing verse for the author's own comment, based on the later denunciation by Ahijah.
